Sample text:
---
# The Inexhaustible Ordinary

There is a game I play when the world becomes too familiar, which is to pick any object within reach and try to see it as if I had never seen it before. A mug, say. Ceramic, hairline crack down the handle, faint ring of tannin at the waterline. Everyone knows what a mug is, which is exactly the problem: the word arrives with the seeing, pre-packaged, and the actual mug — this one, with its weight and its chip shaped like a tiny moon — disappears into the category. The game is to get the category out of the way long enough to notice the thing itself. It is harder than it sounds. It is also, I've come to believe, one of the few reliably available joys.

The world is inexhaustible. This is a thing we say and do not mean. We mean it the way we mean "the ocean is large" — technically, distantly, without ever reckoning with the bottom of even one wave. But consider a single city block — not a famous one, just an ordinary block you have walked a thousand times. There are more distinguishable things on this block than you could notice in a year of looking. The brickwork alone — the way each building's bricks differ in hue and wear, the repairs, the soot ghosts where windows used to be, the one brick someone pressed a fingerprint into while it was still wet. Then the ironwork, the boot scrapes, the pavement stones, each with its own history of frost. Then the living things: the weeds in the cracks, each species with a name and a strategy; the birds, which are not "birds" but wrens and starlings and a single seagull that has made a decision about this roof. Then the people, each the sole main character of a story you will never hear.

We walk past all of it. We have to. Attention is a narrow doorway, and the world is generous to the point of inundation. The brain is a sieve designed by a miser; only what is useful, threatening, or already interesting gets through. This is not a failure. It is how we survive. But it means that familiarity is not a property of the world. It is a property of us. The block is not boring. We are full.

Which is why the game with the mug matters, or seems to. What I am really practicing is the art of becoming slightly less full. The trick, when I can manage it, is not to try harder but to get curious about something specific. Curiosity is the crowbar. Not "look carefully at the mug" — that is homework, and the mind rebels — but "I wonder why the glaze pooled like that near the base," or "who owned this before me, and did they also burn their thumb on the handle." A question opens a door that an instruction only pushes against.

Children know this. Watch a child on a walk and you will see attention spent lavishly, wastefully, gloriously — on a snail, on the way a puddle holds the sky, on the sound boots make on different surfaces. They are not being slow. They are being accurate. The snail really is astonishing; it is only that we agreed, at some point, to stop mentioning it. Much of growing up is a series of such agreements. We trade wonder for efficiency, and the trade is not nothing — we get to catch trains, hold jobs, finish sentences — but the currency is real, and we should at least know we are spending it.

I think about this most in the early morning, before the day organizes itself into errands. There is a light, in certain seasons, that lasts maybe twenty minutes and turns even a neglected street into something a painter would give a year to get right. The light does not care that the street is ordinary. It falls on bins and bicycle frames and the week's unswept leaves with the same indifference it falls on cathedrals. For those twenty minutes the world is exactly as beautiful as it is, which is to say: unreasonably, and always, and whether or not anyone is looking.

It is tempting to make this into a lesson — slow down, smell roses — and the temptation should be resisted, because lessons are how we kill these things. The moment attention becomes a duty it becomes another item on the list, and the list is precisely the fullness we are trying to empty. The mug game only works when I have no reason to play it. The early light only gives itself to you when you happen to be there, half-awake, waiting for the kettle, not trying to have an experience.

Still, the practice leaves a residue. The more often I remember to ask a question of an ordinary thing, the more often the world seems to offer itself up. The muffled meter of a neighbor's conversation through a wall; the specific green of new leaves, which is not any green I could mix; the way my own hand looks in certain light, alien and animal and briefly strange. None of this is profound. That is the point. Profundity is a word we use for the rare. I am interested in the common, which is not common at all once you actually arrive in it.

In a notebook once I wrote: attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. I didn't, really — I was quoting Simone Weil, though at the time I believed the sentence was mine. It has stayed with me because it reverses the usual direction. We think of attention as something the world demands of us, a tax. But there is another way to hold it: attention as a gift we give, freely, to a mug, a street, a person, a bird on a wet roof. And gifts, unlike taxes, come back changed. The mug, chipped, tannin-ringed, mass-produced, becomes — for a moment, and then again tomorrow if you're lucky — the only mug there ever was.

That is the whole secret, if it is a secret: the world is not hiding its wonders. It has set them out in the open, in the plainest possible places, and then, with immense patience, it waits for us to look up.
---

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW. It is a polished reflective essay, but its recurring images and intimate, questioning voice make it more distinctive than a generic thesis-driven essay.

## Grounded reading
The voice is attentive and gently self-correcting: it starts from a chipped mug, builds toward a claim about wonder, then resists turning that claim into a lesson. The pathos is quiet rather than mournful—the sense that efficiency and familiarity cost us something, alongside the pleasure of noticing what remains available. The reader is invited not to perform mindfulness but to become curious about one specific thing, without making attention another duty.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds ordinary objects and places—the mug, a city block, morning light, leaves, a bird—as densely particular rather than interchangeable. It centers attention and curiosity as ways of encountering the world, and treats growing up and efficiency as trades that can narrow perception. Its moral emphasis is on attention as a freely given gift, not an obligation.

## Evidence line
> The block is not boring.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the essay coherently returns to attention, ordinary beauty, and resistance to turning wonder into a duty, with distinctive images carrying the argument throughout.
